analysis.one_liner: Blocks the first federal standard requiring employers to protect workers from extreme heat.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Workforce Committee advanced the bill 18–15 on July 21, 2026; the full House has not yet voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Labor Department from ever finalizing, carrying out, or enforcing OSHA's proposed rule on workplace heat — the first specific federal standard requiring employers to protect workers from heat illness. The rule would apply across general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture, requiring employers to have prevention plans once heat reaches 80°F, with extra protections at 90°F. Instead of this rule, workers would remain protected only by OSHA's broad general-duty authority and its heat inspection program. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Employers in agriculture, construction, warehousing, and other heat-exposed industries would gain, because they would not have to develop and run the heat injury and illness prevention plans the proposed rule requires — plans covering water, shade or cooling, rest breaks, and monitoring once workplace heat reaches 80°F, with extra steps at 90°F. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: It forbids the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed OSHA heat standard — or any substantially similar standard — so the rule can never take effect.

It spares employers across general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture from having to create heat injury and illness prevention plans, including the requirements the rule would impose at the 80°F initial trigger and the 90°F high-heat trigger.

It leaves in place the current system the CRS summary describes: OSHA enforces heat hazards through the 1970 Act's general duty clause and a National Emphasis Program of targeted heat inspections, rather than a binding standard with specific triggers and duties.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in hot jobs — farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers — would bear the cost in the form of continued exposure to workplace heat without a specific, enforceable federal standard; heat illness and deaths fall hardest on them. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Outdoor and warehouse workers facing heat

drawbacks.text: OSHA currently has no specific heat exposure standard, so without the rule, workers are protected only by the general requirement that employers provide a workplace free from recognized hazards — a standard the CRS notes OSHA has applied to heat through citations and a National Emphasis Program, but which sets no specific triggers like water, shade, or rest breaks at 80°F and 90°F.

The bill is written to bar not just this rule but 'any substantially similar standard,' which would prevent OSHA from issuing any comparable heat protection rule in the future, not merely delay this one.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the compliance burden: the rule would require covered employers in all general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture to develop and maintain heat prevention plans, train staff, and provide protections whenever heat hits 80°F, with costlier requirements above 90°F — real expenses, felt most by small operators in low-margin sectors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow one way: employers in agriculture, construction, and other heat-exposed industries avoid the cost of prevention plans, training, and rest-and-water requirements, while the corresponding cost falls on workers who would keep facing extreme heat with no specific federal standard — only OSHA's harder-to-enforce general authority. Blocking a rule permanently, including 'substantially similar' future standards, means the trade-off is not a delay for refinement but the absence of any binding heat protection. The bill is well-targeted at its sponsors' goal of preventing the rule, but the burden it shifts is a health and safety burden on workers. [S2, S3]

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House committee markup 18–15 in July 2026 and now waits to see whether the full House will take it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
On July 21, 2026, the committee held a markup and voted 18–15 to order the bill reported to the House with amendments.
All 68 cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat is listed as a sponsor.

If enacted, the bill would bar the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' rule published August 30, 2024, or any substantially similar standard.
Because the 119th Congress is still in session, the bill has not reached a final outcome; it awaits possible action on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers in heat-exposed industries are better off: the bill that would spare them the rule's compliance requirements cleared committee on a party-line-leaning 18–15 vote, while the proposed heat standard remains blocked only if the bill becomes law. Workers in hot jobs have gained nothing yet, but stand to lose the most if it advances.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 cosponsors are Republicans, and the committee advanced it 18–15, closely tracking the panel's party split.

industries.note: The bill would lift the threat of a binding heat standard covering agricultural employers, who would otherwise have to run prevention plans with water, shade, and rest triggers at 80°F and 90°F. Farm and field workers, who face some of the highest heat risks, would get no specific standard in return.
Construction firms would avoid the cost of heat prevention plans and training the proposed rule would require on outdoor job sites. The saving comes at the expense of crews working in extreme heat.

industries.industry: Warehousing, delivery, and other indoor heat-exposed employers
industries.note: Hot indoor workplaces like warehouses and kitchens fall under the proposed rule's 'indoor work' coverage; the bill would keep that obligation from ever taking effect.

industries.industry: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (federal workplace safety enforcement)
industries.note: OSHA would be barred from issuing or enforcing its first specific heat standard and would have to rely on its existing general-duty citations and National Emphasis Program on heat, which the CRS summary describes as less specific than a binding rule.

analysis.trajectory: With committee approval in hand and a House Republican majority, the bill could reach the House floor, though statutory blocks on pending regulations are uncommon and the Senate path is uncertain. Meanwhile the underlying OSHA rulemaking proceeds on its own track, so the bill's practical effect depends on whether it becomes law before the rule is finalized. [S5]
